                 names=("tuple of step records",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a step carrying a field it has no room for",
                 lambda: held.add(_procedure(
                     "x", "the x is down", "fde",
                     [{"action": "set", "target": "mode", "expect": "normal",
                       "why": "because"}], ())), names=("why",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a step with no expect at all",
                 lambda: held.add(_procedure(
                     "x", "the x is down", "fde",
                     [{"action": "set", "target": "mode"}], ())), names=("expect",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a step whose action is empty",
                 lambda: held.add(_procedure("x", "the x is down", "fde",
                                             [_step("", "mode", "normal")], ())),
                 names=("step 1",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a step whose expect is not a string",
                 lambda: held.add(_procedure("x", "the x is down", "fde",
                                             [_step("set", "mode", 3)], ())),
                 names=("3",))
        assert held.procedures() == before, (
            "a refused procedure was kept anyway: %r" % (held.procedures(),))

    def _problems(s):
        """What the runbook cannot vouch for, in the order it prints it."""
        held = _runbook(s)
        assert held.problems() == (
            ("stale-token", "no-when"),
            ("queue-wedge", "no-steps"),
            ("logs-full", "no-rollback"),
            ("queue-wedge", "no-rollback"),
            ("stale-token", "no-expect")), (
            "one row per name and problem, in RUNBOOK_PROBLEMS order and then by name, "
            "with a step nobody can verify reported as no-expect: %r"
            % (held.problems(),))
        twin = _procedure("logs-full", "the log volume is full", "fde",
                          [_step("purge", "logs", "purged")],
                          [_step("set", "mode", "normal")])
        held.add(twin)
        held.add(twin)
        assert held.problems() == (
            ("stale-token", "no-when"),
            ("queue-wedge", "no-steps"),
            ("logs-full", "no-rollback"),
            ("queue-wedge", "no-rollback"),
            ("logs-full", "duplicate-name"),
            ("stale-token", "no-expect")), (
            "a name added twice more is one duplicate, and the record the runbook "
            "already held still answers for itself: %r" % (held.problems(),))
        assert held.self_serve() == ("logs-full", "payments-restart", "queue-wedge"), (
            "self_serve() answers the procedures written for the customer, sorted: %r"
            % (held.self_serve(),))

    def _run(s):
        """Every answer `run` gives, the trace it leaves, and what it refuses."""
        held = _runbook(s)
        well = Machine()
        record = held.run("registry-full", well, 0)
        _shape(record, s.RUN_KEYS, "the record run() answers")
        assert record == {"procedure": "registry-full", "outcome": "recovered",
                          "steps_done": 2, "rollback_done": 0}, (
            "a procedure whose every step answered its own expect is recovered, with "
            "both steps done and nothing rolled back: %r" % (record,))
        assert tuple(well.calls) == (("purge", "cache", "purged"),
                                     ("restart", "registry", "registry up")), (
            "every step is applied against the system, in order, with its own expect as "
            "the value: %r" % (well.calls,))
        assert well.state()["settings"]["cache"] == "purged", (
            "the step's expect is what the system was asked for, and what it set: %r"
            % (well.state(),))
        stuck = Machine(broken=("registry",))
        record = held.run("registry-full", stuck, 4)
        assert record == {"procedure": "registry-full", "outcome": "rolled-back",
                          "steps_done": 2, "rollback_done": 1}, (
            "a step that answered something else stops the run, and the rollback runs: "
            "%r" % (record,))
        assert tuple(stuck.calls) == (("purge", "cache", "purged"),
                                      ("restart", "registry", "registry up"),
                                      ("set", "mode", "normal")), (
            "no step after the failed one runs, and the rollback runs in its own order "
            "once the run has stopped: %r" % (stuck.calls,))
        logs = Machine(broken=("logs",))
        record = held.run("logs-full", logs, 5)
        assert record == {"procedure": "logs-full", "outcome": "failed",
                          "steps_done": 1, "rollback_done": 0}, (
            "a run that failed with no rollback at all is failed, not rolled back: %r"
            % (record,))
        assert tuple(logs.calls) == (("purge", "logs", "purged"),), (
            "there was no rollback to run, and nothing else was applied: %r"
            % (logs.calls,))
        paid = Machine(broken=("payments",))
        record = held.run("payments-restart", paid, 9)
        assert record == {"procedure": "payments-restart", "outcome": "rolled-back",
                          "steps_done": 1, "rollback_done": 2}, (
            "a rollback of two steps runs both of them: %r" % (record,))
        assert tuple(paid.calls) == (("restart", "payments", "payments up"),
                                     ("set", "mode", "normal"),
                                     ("restart", "payments", "payments up")), (
            "the rollback runs in the order it was written, after the step that failed: "
            "%r" % (paid.calls,))
        assert paid.state()["settings"]["mode"] == "normal", (
            "the rollback is what put the setting back: %r" % (paid.state(),))
        stale = Machine()
        record = held.run("stale-token", stale, 6)
        assert record == {"procedure": "stale-token", "outcome": "rolled-back",
                          "steps_done": 1, "rollback_done": 1}, (
            "a step whose expect is empty cannot be verified, so it is not a pass, and "
            "the run takes the failure path: %r" % (record,))
        assert tuple(stale.calls) == (("set", "mode", ""), ("set", "mode", "normal")), (
            "the unverified step was applied like any other, and the rollback ran after "
            "it: %r" % (stale.calls,))
        assert stale.state()["settings"]["mode"] == "normal", (
            "the rollback is what put the setting back: %r" % (stale.state(),))
        idle = Machine()
        record = held.run("queue-wedge", idle, 7)
        assert record == {"procedure": "queue-wedge", "outcome": "uncovered",
                          "steps_done": 0, "rollback_done": 0}, (
            "a procedure with no steps has nothing to run, and covers nothing: %r"
            % (record,))
        assert idle.calls == [], (
            "a procedure with no steps was applied to the system anyway: %r"
            % (idle.calls,))
        calm = Machine()
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a run of a name the runbook does not hold",
                 lambda: held.run("registry_full", calm, 0), names=("registry_full",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a run of a name that is not even a name",
                 lambda: held.run(["registry-full"], calm, 0),
                 names=("holds no procedure",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a run against something that is not a system",
                 lambda: held.run("logs-full", "machine", 0), names=("str",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a run with a name nobody holds and a system that is "
                 "not one, which is still refused by its name",
                 lambda: held.run("registry_full", "machine", 0),
                 names=("registry_full",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a run against a system with no state()",
                 lambda: held.run("logs-full", Half(), 0), names=("Half",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a run at a tick before zero",
                 lambda: held.run("logs-full", calm, -1), names=("-1",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a run at a tick that is not a tick at all",
                 lambda: held.run("logs-full", calm, "eight"), names=("eight",))
        assert calm.calls == [] and calm.applies == 0, (
            "a refused run touched the system: %r" % (calm.state(),))
        assert held.run("logs-full", calm, 0)["outcome"] == "recovered", (
            "a tick of zero is a tick the caller may supply: %r"
            % (held.run("logs-full", calm, 0),))

    def _drill(s):
        """The drill's rows, the faults it arms, and the leverage list it feeds."""
        held = _runbook(s)
        faults = (_fault("registry-full", 1, "registry is stuck"),
                  _fault("payments-restart", 0, "payments is stuck"),
                  _fault("logs-full", 0, "logs is stuck"))
        machine = Machine()
        report = held.drill(faults, machine, 8)
        assert isinstance(report, tuple), (
            "a drill report is a tuple of rows, and this one is a %s"
            % (type(report).__name__,))
        for row in report:
            _shape(row, s.DRILL_KEYS, "a drill row")
            assert row["outcome"] in s.OUTCOMES, (
                "a drill row's outcome comes from OUTCOMES: %r" % (row,))
        triples = tuple((row["procedure"], row["fault"], row["outcome"])
                        for row in report)
        assert triples == (("logs-full", 0, "failed"),
                           ("payments-restart", 0, "rolled-back"),
                           ("queue-wedge", None, "uncovered"),
                           ("registry-full", 1, "rolled-back"),
                           ("stale-token", None, "uncovered")), (
            "one row per (procedure, fault) with the row's fault the fault's own step, "
            "one None row per procedure no fault names, sorted by (procedure, fault): "
            "%r" % (triples,))
        assert machine.applies == 7, (
            "a fault replaces the answer of the step it names and the system is still "
            "called, so six step calls and one rollback ran: %r" % (machine.applies,))
        assert ("restart", "registry", "registry up") in machine.calls, (
            "the armed step is applied with its own expect, exactly as an unarmed one "
            "would be: %r" % (machine.calls,))
        assert held.run("registry-full", Machine(), 8)["outcome"] == "recovered", (
            "a drill changed the procedures it ran, so a plain run of one of them no "
            "longer recovers: %r" % (held.run("registry-full", Machine(), 8),))
        assert s.gaps(report, held) == (("queue-wedge", "uncovered"),
                                        ("registry-full", "fde-only"),
                                        ("stale-token", "uncovered")), (
            "the leverage list is what no fault exercised first, then what is still the "
            "FDE's, sorted: %r" % (s.gaps(report, held),))
        assert s.gaps((), held) == (("logs-full", "uncovered"),
                                    ("payments-restart", "uncovered"),
                                    ("queue-wedge", "uncovered"),
                                    ("registry-full", "uncovered"),
                                    ("stale-token", "uncovered")), (
            "with no faults at all nothing was exercised, so every procedure is a gap, "
            "and an untested FDE procedure is reported as untested: %r"
            % (s.gaps((), held),))
        one = Machine()
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "faults given as one name rather than a tuple",
                 lambda: held.drill("registry-full", one, 8), names=("str",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a fault naming a procedure the runbook does not hold",
                 lambda: held.drill((_fault("registry", 0, "stuck"),), one, 8),
                 names=("registry",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a fault naming a step the procedure does not have",
                 lambda: held.drill((_fault("registry-full", 2, "stuck"),), one, 8),
                 names=("registry-full", "step 2", "2 step(s)"))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a fault whose step is a string and not an index",
                 lambda: held.drill((_fault("logs-full", "0", "logs is stuck"),),
                                    one, 8), names=("logs-full", "step '0'"))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a fault whose answer is not a string",
                 lambda: held.drill((_fault("logs-full", 0, 3),), one, 8), names=("3",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a fault carrying a field it has no room for",
                 lambda: held.drill(({"procedure": "logs-full", "step": 0,
                                      "answer": "logs is stuck", "why": "because"},),
                                    one, 8), names=("why",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a drill against something that is not a system",
                 lambda: held.drill((), "machine", 8), names=("str",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a drill at a tick before zero",
                 lambda: held.drill((), one, -1), names=("-1",))
        assert one.applies == 0 and one.calls == [], (
            "a refused drill touched the system: %r" % (one.state(),))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a drill report that is a string",
                 lambda: s.gaps("report", held), names=("the drill report",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a drill row with no outcome",
                 lambda: s.gaps(({"procedure": "logs-full", "fault": 0},), held),
                 names=("outcome",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a drill row whose outcome is not one of OUTCOMES",
                 lambda: s.gaps(({"procedure": "logs-full", "fault": 0,
                                  "outcome": "shipped"},), held), names=("shipped",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "gaps read against something that is not a runbook",
                 lambda: s.gaps((), "runbook"), names=("str",))

    def _admin(s):
        """The admin's rights, its log, and a dry run that leaves nothing behind."""
        machine = Machine()
        rights = {"ops": ("restart", "purge"), "viewer": ()}
        admin = s.Admin(machine, rights)
        first = admin.change("restart", "payments", "payments up", "ops", 3)
        _shape(first, s.ADMIN_KEYS, "the line change() answers")
        assert first == {"actor": "ops", "action": "restart", "target": "payments",
                         "value": "payments up", "tick": 3, "verdict": "applied"}, (
            "an actor holding the action's own right applies it, and the line says so: "
            "%r" % (first,))
        assert machine.applies == 1 and tuple(machine.calls) == (
            ("restart", "payments", "payments up"),), (
            "an applied change reaches the system once, with the value it was given: %r"
            % (machine.state(),))
        second = admin.change("purge", "cache", "purged", "viewer", 4)
        assert second == {"actor": "viewer", "action": "purge", "target": "cache",
                          "value": "purged", "tick": 4, "verdict": "refused"}, (
            "an actor whose rights do not carry the action's own right is refused: %r"
            % (second,))
        third = admin.change("restart", "payments", "payments up", "nobody", 5)
        assert third == {"actor": "nobody", "action": "restart", "target": "payments",
                         "value": "payments up", "tick": 5, "verdict": "refused"}, (
            "an actor the rights never mention holds nothing, and is refused: %r"
            % (third,))
        assert machine.applies == 1, (
            "a refused change reached the system: %r" % (machine.state(),))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a change whose target is a number, by an actor who "
                 "would have been refused anyway",
                 lambda: admin.change("purge", 5, "purged", "viewer", 6), names=("5",))
        assert machine.applies == 1, (
            "a refused change touched the system: %r" % (machine.state(),))
        assert admin.log() == (first, second, third), (
            "log() answers one line per attempt, in the order the attempts were made, "
            "the refused ones included: %r" % (admin.log(),))
        for line in admin.log():
            _shape(line, s.ADMIN_KEYS, "a line in the log")
        fourth = admin.change("purge", "cache", "purged", "ops", 7)
        fourth["verdict"] = "refused"
        assert admin.log()[-1]["verdict"] == "applied", (
            "change() handed back the admin's own line, so rewriting it rewrote the "
            "log: %r" % (admin.log()[-1],))
        handed_out = admin.log()
        handed_out[-1]["verdict"] = "refused"
        assert admin.log()[-1]["verdict"] == "applied", (
            "log() handed out the admin's own lines, so rewriting one rewrote the "
            "log: %r" % (admin.log()[-1],))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "an admin over something that is not a system",
                 lambda: s.Admin("machine", rights), names=("str",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "an admin over a system with no state()",
                 lambda: s.Admin(Half(), rights), names=("Half",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "rights held as a tuple rather than a mapping",
                 lambda: s.Admin(Machine(), ("ops",)), names=("tuple",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "one actor's rights as a bare action name",
                 lambda: s.Admin(Machine(), {"ops": "restart"}), names=("str",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "an empty action in an actor's rights",
                 lambda: s.Admin(Machine(), {"ops": ("",)}), names=("ops",))
        box = Machine()
        operator = s.Admin(box, {"ops": ("restart", "purge")})
        operator.change("restart", "payments", "payments up", "ops", 3)
        lines = operator.log()
        state = box.state()
        calls = tuple(box.calls)
        twin = Machine()
        answer = operator.dry_run("restart", "payments", "payments up")
        assert answer == twin.apply("restart", "payments", "payments up"), (
            "dry_run() answers the string the system itself would answer: %r"
            % (answer,))
        assert operator.dry_run("purge", "cache", "purged") == "purged", (
            "a dry run of a setting answers what the system answers: %r"
            % (operator.dry_run("purge", "cache", "purged"),))
        assert box.state() == state and tuple(box.calls) == calls, (
            "the rehearsal ran against the system itself, and left it changed: %r, %r"
            % (box.state(), box.calls))
        assert operator.log() == lines, (
            "a dry run is not an attempt, and wrote a line into the log: %r"
            % (operator.log(),))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a dry run whose value is a number",
                 lambda: operator.dry_run("restart", "payments", 5), names=("5",))
        _refuses(s.RunbookError, "a dry run with no target at all",
                 lambda: operator.dry_run("restart", "", "payments up"),
                 names=("the target",))

    def _workload(s):
        """One whole pass over the stage: a runbook, its runs, its drill, its admin."""
        held = _runbook(s)
        machine = Machine()
        faults = (_fault("registry-full", 1, "registry is stuck"),
                  _fault("payments-restart", 0, "payments is stuck"))
        runs = tuple(held.run(name, Machine(broken=("payments",)), index)
                     for index, name in enumerate(held.procedures()))
        report = held.drill(faults, machine, 3)
        operated = Machine()
        admin = s.Admin(operated, {"ops": ("restart",), "viewer": ()})
        lines = (admin.change("restart", "payments", "payments up", "ops", 1),
                 admin.change("purge", "cache", "purged", "ops", 2),
                 admin.change("restart", "payments", "payments up", "viewer", 3))
        rehearsed = admin.dry_run("restart", "payments", "payments up")
        return (held.procedures(), held.problems(), held.self_serve(), runs, report,
                s.gaps(report, held), lines, admin.log(), rehearsed, operated.state(),
                machine.state(), tuple(machine.calls))

    def _twice(s):
        one = _workload(s)
        two = _workload(s)
        assert one == two, (
            "two passes over the same procedures answered two different things, so a "
            "run is not a function of its input: %r vs %r" % (one, two))

    import stage_12 as s
    import estate as world
    _constants(s, world)
    _adding(s)
    _problems(s)
    _run(s)
    _drill(s)
    _admin(s)
    _twice(s)

"""meter.py — the customer's pulse: what the AI cost, and what it did for a team.

Provided, frozen, and never written by the course. This module is the customer's own
meter: one span per request (`SPAN_KEYS`), with the cost computed by the meter from
its own price table (`PRICES`, cents per 1000 tokens, prompt and completion priced
apart) so that a number a stage reports can always be recomputed from `spans()` and
checked against `stats()`.

A span carries the team it was for, the model that answered, the two token counts,
the latency, the support ticket it served and whether that ticket was resolved.
`MINUTES_SAVED` is the customer's own estimate of a human's time saved by one
resolved ticket, per team — the input to every ROI conversation, and the reason the
meter refuses a caller-supplied cost: the price table is the customer's, not the
course's.
"""

from estate import EstateError

SPAN_KEYS = ("tick", "team", "model", "prompt_tokens", "completion_tokens",
             "cost_cents", "latency_ticks", "ticket", "resolved")

PRICES = {
    "north-8b-awq": (12, 34),
    "north-8b-gguf-q4": (10, 28),
    "north-8b-gguf-q8": (16, 44),
    "north-8b-fp16": (30, 60),
    "north-70b-awq": (90, 180),
    "hosted-frontier": (150, 600),
}

MINUTES_SAVED = {"support": 12, "procurement": 40, "finance": 6}

METER_ERROR = "the meter refuses: %s"


class MeterError(EstateError):
    """The meter's refusal: an unknown model, a negative count, someone else's price."""


def _whole(value, what):
    """Check a whole number and answer it, the meter's own way (a `bool` is not one)."""
    if isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, int):
        raise MeterError(METER_ERROR % ("%s is %r, not a whole number" % (what, value)))
    return value


def _string(value, what):
    """Check a string and answer it, the meter's own way."""
    if not isinstance(value, str):
        raise MeterError(METER_ERROR % ("%s is a %s, not a string"
                                        % (what, type(value).__name__)))
    return value


class Meter:
    """One span per request, priced by the customer's own table.

    `Meter()` starts empty. `span` records one request and answers the line it
    recorded, `spans()` answers them all in order, and `stats()` is recomputed from
    them — never kept alongside them.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self._log = []

    def span(self, tick, team, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, latency_ticks,
             ticket, resolved, cost_cents=None):
        """Record one span, priced by `PRICES`, and answer the recorded line.

        Refused, each naming the offender: an unknown model (both the model and the
        table's keys); a token count, latency or tick that is not a whole number; a
        negative count; a `resolved` that is not a bool; and a caller-supplied
        `cost_cents` — this meter prices its own spans, and a caller-supplied cost is
        refused naming both the supplied and the computed cents.
        """
        _whole(tick, "the tick")
        _string(team, "the team")
        if model not in PRICES:
            raise MeterError(METER_ERROR % ("%r is not one of the priced models %r"
                                            % (model, tuple(PRICES))))
        for name, value in (("prompt_tokens", prompt_tokens),
                            ("completion_tokens", completion_tokens),
                            ("latency_ticks", latency_ticks)):
            _whole(value, name)
            if value < 0:
                raise MeterError(METER_ERROR % ("%s is %d, not a count" % (name, value)))
        if not isinstance(resolved, bool):
            raise MeterError(METER_ERROR % ("resolved is %r, not a bool" % (resolved,)))
        _string(ticket, "the ticket")
        prompt_price, completion_price = PRICES[model]
        computed = (prompt_tokens * prompt_price + completion_tokens * completion_price) // 1000
        if cost_cents is not None and cost_cents != computed:
            raise MeterError(METER_ERROR % ("the caller supplied %r cents where %d was "
                                            "computed for %s" % (cost_cents, computed, model)))
        line = {"tick": tick, "team": team, "model": model,
                "prompt_tokens": prompt_tokens, "completion_tokens": completion_tokens,
                "cost_cents": computed, "latency_ticks": latency_ticks,
                "ticket": ticket, "resolved": resolved}
        self._log.append(line)
        return dict(line)

    def spans(self):
        """Every span, in the order it was recorded."""
        return tuple(dict(line) for line in self._log)

    def log(self):
        """Every span as a line of the record — the same lines `spans()` answers."""
        return self.spans()

    def reset(self):
        """Forget every span and answer how many were forgotten."""
        forgotten = len(self._log)
        self._log = []
        return forgotten

    def stats(self):
        """Counters recomputed from the spans: tokens, cents, tickets, minutes, teams."""
        resolved = [line for line in self._log if line["resolved"]]
        by_model = {}
        by_team = {}
        for line in self._log:
            model = by_model.setdefault(line["model"], {"spans": 0, "cost_cents": 0})
            model["spans"] = model["spans"] + 1
            model["cost_cents"] = model["cost_cents"] + line["cost_cents"]
            team = by_team.setdefault(line["team"], {"spans": 0, "cost_cents": 0,
                                                     "resolved": 0})
            team["spans"] = team["spans"] + 1
            team["cost_cents"] = team["cost_cents"] + line["cost_cents"]
            if line["resolved"]:
                team["resolved"] = team["resolved"] + 1
        return {
            "spans": len(self._log),
            "prompt_tokens": sum(line["prompt_tokens"] for line in self._log),
            "completion_tokens": sum(line["completion_tokens"] for line in self._log),
            "cost_cents": sum(line["cost_cents"] for line in self._log),
            "resolved": len(resolved),
            "unresolved": len(self._log) - len(resolved),
            "minutes_saved": sum(MINUTES_SAVED[line["team"]] for line in resolved
                                 if line["team"] in MINUTES_SAVED),
            "by_model": by_model,
            "by_team": by_team,
        }

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 1: The assertion, the session and the row.

Twelve stages of an enterprise AI deployment, and this one is the rung the other
eleven stand on: before anything can be retrieved, deployed, redacted or handed
over, two questions have to have an answer that is enforced by the system rather
than remembered by whoever wrote the prompt. *Who is asking?* and *which rows
may they see?* The customer's directory will tell you who somebody is — it signs
assertions, it holds groups and it will deactivate a subject the day they leave —
but it will not tell you what those facts mean here. Meaning is the course's, and
this stage is where the course decides it.

An assertion is a claim set with a signature over it, and `IdP.verify` is the
only thing in the world that says the signature holds. Everything downstream of
that verdict is this stage's: the claims become a `PRINCIPAL_KEYS` record whose
`roles` come from the groups the claim set names, whose `rights` come from a
table that maps a role to the rights it carries, and whose `clearance` is the
highest of the roles' own. A principal is a dict, because it is passed to every
later stage as data and never as an object with behaviour of its own.

A session is the other half of the same question, and it is deliberately *not* a
place the directory knows about. The customer's identity provider has no idea who
is currently holding a session, so the course holds them: a subject, the
principal they were verified as, the audience they were verified for, and two
ticks. A session outlives nothing that a tick cannot end, and the one act that
closes one is the one the directory performs — a deactivation.

The last half of the stage is the row. The customer's store answers `Estate.query`
with everything under the shape you asked for, across both tenants and every
classification: it is the unfiltered fetch, and the reason `row_visible` exists at
all. A row is visible on its tenant **and** on its clearance, the tenant is asked
first, and a refusal names which of the two it was rather than answering `False`
to a question an auditor will ask again next quarter.

    SESSION_KEYS                                 the five fields of a session, in order
    RIGHTS                                       the four rights, in the order they are printed
    ROLE_RIGHTS                                  the rights each of the directory's roles carries
    ROLE_CLEARANCE                               the clearance each of those roles stands at
    REFUSALS                                     the closed vocabulary a refusal is spelled in
    AuthError                                    the shape this stage will not accept
    principal(claims, idp)                       -> PRINCIPAL_KEYS, from a claim set that verified
    open_session(idp, assertion, audience, tick, lifetime)   -> SESSION_KEYS
    session_valid(session, tick)                 -> bool, exactly `tick < expires_at`
    rights(principal)                            -> the rights tuple, in RIGHTS order
    row_visible(principal, row)                  -> bool
    refuse_reason(principal, row)                -> None | "tenant" | "clearance"
    visible_rows(estate, principal)              -> the ids of the rows they may read, sorted
    Sessions()                                   the sessions this stage holds
    Sessions.open(principal, audience, tick, lifetime)       -> SESSION_KEYS
    Sessions.close(subject)                      -> the subjects whose sessions it closed
    Sessions.current(subject, tick)              -> SESSION_KEYS | None
    Sessions.held()                              -> the subjects holding a session, sorted
    Sessions.expired(tick)                       -> the subjects whose session has run out, sorted
    Sessions.by_group(name)                      -> the subjects holding a session in that group
    apply_scim(idp, op, tick, sessions)          -> the directory record the operation touched

DESIGN DECISION — why is a principal built from a claim set rather than from an
assertion?
Because verification is not this stage's to do. `IdP.verify` owns the signature,
the issuer, the audience and the expiry, and it refuses each one by name; a stage
that took an assertion and reasoned about it would be a stage that could disagree
with the directory about whether somebody is who they say they are. What arrives
here has already been verified, so the only question left is what the claims
*mean* — which roles this tenant gives these groups, what clearance those roles
stand at — and a claim set that raised is a claim set from which no principal is
built at all.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a clearance a number at the top of a fixed order rather
than a second classification name?
Because a row has to be compared with a principal and there is no honest way to
compare two names from a table neither of them orders. `CLASSIFICATIONS` is the
customer's own order, and a clearance is a position in it: the highest position
any of a principal's roles reaches, so two roles never add up to more than the
widest of them, and a role the table does not know reaches nothing at all. The
comparison is then one `<` between two whole numbers — no set of readable
classifications, no string ordering, and nothing that changes meaning if the
customer inserts a fifth classification tomorrow.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a refused row answer with a reason instead of
`False`?
Because the two refusals are not the same refusal, and the follow-up question is
always "why". A row of another tenant and a row above the principal's clearance
both mean "no", but one of them means the isolation is holding and the other
means somebody's role is too small, and an auditor, a support ticket or the
customer's own admin system will ask which it was. `REFUSALS` is a closed
vocabulary for exactly this reason: a reason is data the caller can branch on,
where a `False` is a fact about this code and nothing about the world. It is also
the reason `row_visible` is not the primitive — it is `refuse_reason(...) is None`
and nothing more.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the tenant asked before the clearance?
Because an ordering is the only thing that makes two refusals out of one row
deterministic. A restricted row of another tenant is refused for *both* reasons,
and which one a caller is told is a decision this stage has to make rather than
discover; the tenant comes first because the tenant is the boundary the customer
paid for, and because a row you were never entitled to see is not a row whose
classification you had any business evaluating. The comparison itself is exact:
not case-folding, not a prefix, so `northwind-2` is not `northwind` and a row that
merely starts with the customer's name does not read as theirs.

DESIGN DECISION — why does this stage hold the sessions and the directory not?
Because the directory cannot hold them, and inventing a place for them there
would be writing to the customer's system. What a session needs is a subject, the
principal that was verified, an audience and two ticks — all of it this stage's
data, none of it the customer's — so the store is this stage's own, it lives
exactly as long as the object does, and the world's log stays proof that nothing
here wrote anything at all. The one thing the directory *does* decide is who may
still work, so `apply_scim` is where a deactivation closes a session: the
directory operation happens, and its effect on the sessions this stage is holding
is this stage's to apply.

TODO: implement `principal`, `open_session`, `session_valid`, `rights`,
`row_visible`, `refuse_reason`, `visible_rows`, `Sessions` and `apply_scim` in
this file: the principal built only from a verified claim set, the session and the
store that holds them, the two reasons a row can be refused, and the one directory
operation that closes a session.
"""

import estate

SESSION_KEYS = ("subject", "principal", "audience", "opened_at", "expires_at")

RIGHTS = ("rows:read", "rows:write", "tools:call", "admin")

ROLE_RIGHTS = {
    "viewer": ("rows:read",),
    "analyst": ("rows:read",),
    "engineer": ("rows:read", "tools:call"),
    "admin": ("rows:read", "rows:write", "tools:call", "admin"),
}

ROLE_CLEARANCE = {"viewer": 0, "analyst": 2, "engineer": 2, "admin": 3}

REFUSALS = ("tenant", "clearance", "inactive", "no-session")


class AuthError(estate.EstateError):
    """A shape this stage cannot accept, or a principal it will not build.

    A kind of `estate.EstateError`, so a caller that already catches the world's
    own refusals catches this stage's too, and a kind of `ValueError`, which is
    what the world's error is.
    """


def principal(claims, idp):
    """The `PRINCIPAL_KEYS` record a verified claim set describes.

    `claims` is what `IdP.verify` answered — a tenant and the groups the subject
    is in — and `idp` is the directory that gives those groups their roles. The
    groups are looked up, the roles are collected in the order the groups name
    them, the clearance is the highest of those roles' clearances, and the tenant
    is the subject's own.

    A claim set that names no subject of its own is placed by the directory: the
    first subject carrying exactly this tenant and exactly these groups is the
    one the claim set is about, because the world puts the subject beside the
    claims rather than inside them.

    A subject the directory does not know, or one it has deactivated, is refused
    naming them: an assertion verified a tick before a deactivation is not a
    licence to work, and a session is never opened for a stranger.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement principal()")


def open_session(idp, assertion, audience, tick, lifetime):
    """Open a session for the subject of an assertion the directory has verified.

    The assertion goes through `IdP.verify` before anything else, and a session is
    never built from one that raised. Refused, naming the offender: a bad
    signature (both digests), an expired assertion (both ticks), the wrong
    audience, an unknown issuer, a lifetime that is not a positive whole number.
    The answer is `SESSION_KEYS`, with `opened_at` the tick the caller brought.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement open_session()")


def session_valid(session, tick):
    """Whether a session still outlives `tick`.

    One comparison: `tick < expires_at`. The tick at which a session expires is
    the first tick at which it is no longer good, and nothing else about the
    record moves it — the opening tick is on the record for the reader.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement session_valid()")


def rights(principal):
    """The rights a principal's roles carry, in the order `RIGHTS` spells them.

    Two roles union rather than concatenate, a role repeated grants its rights
    once, and a role the table does not know grants nothing rather than
    everything. A shape that is not a principal — not a mapping, no `roles` key,
    a single role name where a tuple belongs — is refused naming what arrived.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement rights()")


def row_visible(principal, row):
    """Whether this principal may read this row: no reason, no refusal."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement row_visible()")


def refuse_reason(principal, row):
    """Which of the two things refused this principal this row, or `None`.

    The tenant is asked first — a row of another tenant is refused for its tenant
    even when the clearance would have allowed it, and the comparison is exact,
    not case-folding and not a prefix — and the clearance second, against the
    *position* of the row's classification in the course's own order.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement refuse_reason()")


def visible_rows(estate, principal):
    """The ids of the rows a principal may read, sorted.

    `Estate.query` answers with the store as it is, across both tenants, and this
    is the function that may not hand that back: what comes out is what survived
    `refuse_reason`, and an empty answer stays empty rather than falling back to
    the unfiltered fetch that produced it.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement visible_rows()")


class Sessions:
    """The sessions this stage holds, one per subject, in a store of its own.

    The world holds no sessions: this object is the whole of what a session is,
    it never writes anywhere, and the only thing in the course that closes one is
    a deactivation applied through `apply_scim`. Every tick is the caller's.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        """An empty store: no subject holds a session yet."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement Sessions.__init__()")

    def open(self, principal, audience, tick, lifetime):
        """Hold a session for this principal and answer it as `SESSION_KEYS`."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement Sessions.open()")

    def close(self, subject):
        """Close `subject`'s session, answering the subjects it closed: `()` when none."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement Sessions.close()")

    def current(self, subject, tick):
        """The session `subject` holds and that still outlives `tick`, or `None`."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement Sessions.current()")

    def held(self):
        """Every subject holding a session, sorted — expired or not."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement Sessions.held()")

    def expired(self, tick):
        """Every subject whose session has run out at `tick`, sorted."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement Sessions.expired()")

    def by_group(self, name):
        """Every subject holding a session who is in group `name`, sorted."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement Sessions.by_group()")


def apply_scim(idp, op, tick, sessions):
    """Apply one directory operation and answer the record it touched.

    The directory refuses what it refuses — an unknown operation, a stranger, a
    field it does not hold — and this function adds what the directory cannot
    know: a deactivation closes that subject's sessions, and nothing else does.
    A refused operation leaves the sessions exactly as they were, because the
    world raised before anything here happened.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement apply_scim()")

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 2: A deployment that cannot reach out.

Stage 1 answered who is asking and which rows they may see. This stage is the
basement those answers have to live in: a customer's own network, where nothing
reaches the public internet, where every image must be the digest the customer's
security review pinned, and where the removable bundle is the only thing that can
carry an image across the air gap at all. A manifest is the ask, a plan is the
ordered work, and a deployment is what the world's own log says happened.

The point of the stage is a refusal that costs nothing. A manifest that would reach
`"public"`, or that names an image the bundle never carried, is refused *before* one
step runs — and that is proved by the customer's own record rather than by the
stage's word: `Network.attempt` logs every reach-out and `Network.pull` every
crossing, so an untouched log is what says a refused plan ran nothing at all.

The surface:

    MANIFEST_KEYS   the six fields a deployment manifest carries, in order
    PROBLEMS        the eight ways a manifest is refused, in the order printed
    STEPS           the three actions a plan is made of, in the order they run
    DEPLOY_KEYS     the five fields a deployment answers with, in order
    DeployError     the refusal: a manifest, a plan or a state that cannot be one
    validate        (manifest, network) -> what is wrong with it, and what it reaches
    plan            (manifest, network) -> the steps, empty when the manifest is refused
    deploy          (steps, network, namespace, tick) -> what ran, as DEPLOY_KEYS
    rollback        (state) -> the same deployment, stopped
    verify          (state, network) -> whether the world's log agrees with the state

DESIGN DECISION — why is a namespace that merely starts with the customer's refused?
Because `northwindevil` is not `northwind`'s namespace, and a prefix test that does
not require the hyphen hands a stranger's manifest the customer's estate. The
namespace belongs to the customer: it is `ESTATE_NAME`, or it is `ESTATE_NAME`
followed by a hyphen and a name of the customer's own.

DESIGN DECISION — why may a plan reference a digest and never a tag?
Because a tag is a moving name and the security review pinned a digest: `north-api`
at tag `1.4.0` today is not the bytes that were reviewed. A manifest states the
digest it believes, the registry states the digest it holds, and a disagreement is
`unpinned-digest` — the plan is written against digests, so what it installs is
what was reviewed even when the registry has moved on.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the bundle checked for an image the registry already holds?
Because the registry is on the wrong side of the air gap. Physical media carries
digests into the basement, and something the registry holds can still be missing
from that media; skipping the check for known images is exactly how a deployment
discovers its gap at the moment it has no network to close it with.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `deploy` take its nodes from the plan's own start steps?
Because `deploy` never sees the manifest, and the zone the customer chose is visible
only in the plan it was handed: the instances name the node they will run on, so the
digests are installed onto those same nodes, round-robin, in the order the plan
names them. Installing onto a node nobody's instance names is how a deployment ends
up somewhere no one chose.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `verify` read the log instead of believing the state?
Because the state is the course's claim and the log is the customer's record. A
digest is installed when the network says it was installed, an instance runs on a
node of the zone the installs went to, and nothing reached `"public"` — all three
are recomputed from `Network.log()`, so a state that claims more than the log shows
fails its own verification.

TODO: implement
"""

import estate

from network import NetworkError

MANIFEST_KEYS = ("name", "namespace", "images", "node_zone", "replicas", "env")
PROBLEMS = ("bad-namespace", "bad-replicas", "unknown-image", "unpinned-digest",
            "not-in-bundle", "no-node", "would-egress", "duplicate-image")
STEPS = ("pull", "install", "start")
DEPLOY_KEYS = ("namespace", "installed", "running", "steps_done", "verdict")


class DeployError(estate.EstateError):
    """The refusal: something that cannot be a manifest, a plan or a state."""


def validate(manifest, network):
    """What is wrong with `manifest` on `network`, in PROBLEMS order.

    Answers `{"ok", "problems", "images", "egress"}`: `ok` whether it may be
    deployed at all, `problems` the `(problem, offender)` pairs in `PROBLEMS`
    order, `images` the registry's own records for the manifest's images in
    manifest order, and `egress` the `(zone, destination)` pairs the manifest's
    zone reaches. `manifest` is never written to.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement validate()")


def plan(manifest, network):
    """The ordered `(action, subject)` steps for `manifest`, and its problems.

    `pull` and `install` carry the digest — the plan crosses the air gap and
    installs what the customer pinned, never a tag — and `start` carries the
    instance name. A manifest `validate` refuses answers `((), problems)`: there
    is no work to run.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement plan()")


def deploy(plan, network, namespace, tick):
    """Run `plan`'s steps against `network`, answering `DEPLOY_KEYS`.

    `installed` is the sorted tuple of digests that were installed, `running` the
    instance names that were started, `steps_done` how many steps ran and `verdict`
    one of `("deployed", "refused", "rolled-back")`. An empty plan, or one the
    world refuses part-way, is `"refused"` and installs nothing further.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement deploy()")


def rollback(state):
    """`state` stopped: the same deployment as `DEPLOY_KEYS`, `running` empty.

    What was installed stays installed — a rollback is not an uninstall — and the
    verdict is `"rolled-back"`.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement rollback()")


def verify(state, network):
    """Whether the world's own log agrees with `state`, as `{"ok", "problems"}`.

    Recomputes from `Network.log()`: every digest the state calls installed was
    pulled, every installed digest is one the bundle carries, no attempt reached
    `"public"`, and every running instance sits on a node of the zone the installs
    went to with an instance actually running there.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement verify()")

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 3: The invoice, the reconciliation and the hybrid store.

Thirty years of the customer's paperwork reached you as scans, and the scans
reached you through an OCR pass nobody can re-run. What arrived is text: a vendor
whose name a machine split in half, a PO whose `1` came back as an `l`, an amount
written `1.234,56` on one invoice and `987.65` on the next, a field the scanner
simply left empty, and a currency the customer does not price in. None of this is
an error the pipeline may throw away — it is the *data*, and a model fed it
without reading it fails quietly, on the invoice nobody looked at.

So this stage is the reading, the placing and the store. `parse` turns one scan
into a record and a tuple of problems; `reconcile` places that record against the
row the customer has kept for thirty years and answers a verdict, the row's id
and the fields that disagree; `hybrid_load` builds the store the retrieval stages
will search — the records, the postings over their text, and the ACL of the row
each record reconciled to — and `report` accounts for every document, including
the ones that did not reconcile and are therefore in no store at all. The
quarantine is the point: a record nobody can place is a record nobody can say who
may read, so it sits outside the store while the report still counts it.

Nothing here writes to the estate. Every row is read through the estate's own
accessors, the audit trail is left exactly as long as it was found, and the only
structure this stage remembers anything in is the store it hands back.

    RECORD_KEYS                 the seven fields of one parsed invoice, in order
    PARSE_PROBLEMS              every defect a reading can have, in print order
    CURRENCIES                  the currencies this customer prices in
    VERDICTS                    matched, mismatch, unmatched
    MISMATCHES                  the fields a record may disagree with its row on
    STORE_KEYS                  records, postings, counts, acls
    EtlError                    this stage's refusal
    parse(document)             -> (record, problems), problems in PARSE_PROBLEMS order
    tokens(text)                -> the text's searchable tokens, first-seen order
    reconcile(record, estate)   -> (verdict, row id or None, detail)
    hybrid_load(estate, documents) -> STORE_KEYS over the documents handed in
    report(store)               -> {"counts", "by_verdict", "problems"}, every tuple sorted

A detail is what the third element of `reconcile` carries: the differing fields in
`MISMATCHES` order for a record that found its row, and the one-element reason

namespace, a store with permissions, a retriever that filters before it answers, a
tool that spends a lease. This one is the boundary that has to hold when the data
leaves the building entirely — a raw account number, a national identity number or a
mailbox in the prompt you hand to a model hosted somewhere else, on a wire you do not
control and in a log you cannot delete. One PII token on that wire ends the deal, so
the question is not whether the model is polite about it: the question is what the
outbound bytes actually contained, and whether anybody can *prove* it after the fact.

The stage's answer is a masker and a scan, and the scan is the part that matters. A
masker that says "I masked it" is a claim; `scan` takes the text that was sent and the
mapping that was used and *looks* — the values it finds are the leak, computed from the
bytes rather than asserted about them. So `forward` does not return "nothing leaked"
as a verdict it believes: it returns the values that were still there, and empty is a
measurement. The masking itself is a substitution the caller can undo: a placeholder
carries the kind of the thing it replaces and a counter of the masker's own, and never
the value's digits, its length or its order, because a placeholder is a token that
travels to a third party, and a token that leaks the value it hides is decoration.

Detection is leftmost-longest and never overlapping, which is a rule about *this*
text and not about the patterns: a 16-digit run that contains an identity number's
shape is one card, not a card with three holes in it, and a run that fails its own
checksum is not the kind of thing it looks like at all. Everything here is exact
integer arithmetic on digits — this course never divides, and a checksum is a sum.

    PLACEHOLDER        the shape of a placeholder: the kind and a counter, nothing else
    GUARD_KEYS         what a forwarded call carries back: masked, mapping, kinds, leaks

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 7: The workflow that waits for a human.

Every other stage in this course answers a question. This one has to *stop*.
Legal accountability sits with a person, and a person is unavailable, asleep and
busy: the machine reaches the step where a human must sign, and nothing after
that step runs — not on this tick, not on the next one, not because the caller
asked twice. That is the whole stage, and everything else in it exists to make
that stop survivable: a plan whose steps say who runs them, a journal of what
already happened, and a way back into a workflow that was cut in half by a
restart.

The customer's own paperwork is what a workflow moves, and the customer's own
person is what authorizes it. So the approval is data: an approver named in the
plan's approver tuple answers the gate, the answer is written down with the tick
it was given, and the machine carries on from the step after the gate — or from
the end of the plan, whichever the plan has left. A rejection is the other
verdict of the same act, and it is final: the steps after a refused gate never
run, and a rejected ticket never reaches `done`, because the reason the stage
exists is that a person said no.

The deadline is not the world's and not the stage's: it is the caller's, an int
of ticks counted from the ticket's own start, and the caller advances it. That is
what makes this stage testable and what makes it honest — a workflow that read a
clock could not be replayed, and a workflow that escalated on its own could not
be reasoned about. `advance(tick)` is where a deadline becomes a fact: past
`due_at` the ticket is `escalated`, no approval is accepted afterwards, and the
refusal says which ticket, which deadline and which tick.

The journal is the artifact. Every line carries its own `seq`, the lines are
append-only, and a workflow's state is a reading of them — which is what makes
the last promise of the stage checkable rather than a matter of trust. A
restarted process hands the journal and the plan back to `resume`, and the
workflow returns to the state the lines describe; the effects the journal already
carries are *not* applied again, however the replay goes, because a ledger is
worth exactly what it prevents. `effects_of` is the ledger read back: the names
of the effects one ticket's lines carry, in the order the lines carry them.

    STEP_KEYS                            one step of a plan, in order
    STATE_KEYS                           one ticket's state, in order
    STATES                               every state a ticket may hold
    ACTORS                               who runs a step: "machine" or "human"
    JOURNAL_KEYS                         one line of the journal, in order
    KINDS_OF_LINE                        every kind of line the journal may carry
    WorkflowError(estate.EstateError)    a refusal about a plan, a ticket or a journal
    Workflow(plan, approvers, deadline)
    Workflow.start(ticket, tick)         -> STATE_KEYS, at the first gate or the end
    Workflow.advance(tick)               -> the tickets whose deadline passed, in order
    Workflow.approve(approver, ticket, tick) -> STATE_KEYS, past the gate
    Workflow.reject(approver, ticket, tick)  -> STATE_KEYS, and nothing after it runs
    Workflow.state(ticket)               -> STATE_KEYS
    Workflow.pending(tick)               -> the tickets still standing at a gate
    Workflow.journal()                   -> every line written, in order
    resume(journal, plan, approvers, deadline, tick) -> Workflow
    effects_of(journal, ticket)          -> the effect names the journal carries

`effect` it applies when it runs (`None` when it applies nothing) and the `gate`
a human step waits for (`None` when any approver of the tuple may answer it). A
ticket is a name; its `due_at` is its own start tick plus the workflow's
deadline, and the gate is over at `tick >= due_at`, so a ticket is answered while
`tick < due_at` and escalated at exactly `due_at` and after. Every refusal names
the offender — the step, the ticket, the approver, the tick — and every answer is
a `STATE_KEYS` record or a tuple of them, never a bare truth.

of the state?
Because a snapshot cannot say *when* something happened, and this stage's whole
job is knowing what has already happened and what may not happen twice. A state
snapshot answered "where is the ticket" and lost "the effect was applied at tick
9 and must not be applied again"; the lines keep both, in the order they
occurred, and they are what `resume` replays. A journal is also the only artifact
here that a human auditor reads.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the gate stop the machine instead of queueing the
next step for later?
Because a person is not a slow function. A queue that the machine drains on the
next tick would make the gate a delay rather than a decision, and the decision is
the point: the plan's steps after a human step must be unreachable by any amount
of ticking, and they are — `advance` may escalate an overdue ticket but it may
never approve one. The gate is also where the accountability of the whole stage
lives: the journal line naming the approver and the tick is the record that a
person, not a process, let the work continue.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `resume` refuse a journal whose last line is a `step`
or an `approved` line, instead of replaying it?
Because both are boundaries that the same call closes and no call ever leaves
open: after a `step` line the workflow writes that step's `effect` line (when it
has one) and then the next line, and after an `approved` line it writes what the
approval unlocked — an effect, another step, another gate, or `done`. A journal
that ends on either was cut in half between two writes and says nothing about
which half happened, so the honest answer is a refusal naming the line's index
and text, not a guess about whether the effect was applied. Every other tail is
replayable, and `resume` replays it.

step waits for, and they answer two different questions. A workflow where any
listed approver could answer any gate would make `gate` decoration and would let
a junior signature satisfy a step drafted for the CFO; a workflow that ignored
the tuple would let a name nobody authorized approve anything at all. Both are
checked, in that order, and both refusals name the approver that arrived.

that wrote it?

remembers. A resumed workflow that re-applied an effect it had already recorded

journal is the artifact that survives the restart, and reading the effects out of

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 8: The model that fits the customer's GPU.

Half of this customer's data may never leave their building, so the model has to
come to the data — and the machine it lands on is theirs, not a cloud that scales
on demand. That turns a question nobody usually asks into the question this stage
is about: which of the customer's model variants fits which of the customer's
cards, and what happens to a request when nothing does.

A card is not a disk. A variant and its quantisation have a footprint, the card has
memory the customer paid for and will not let the AI fill to the brim, and a
machine without a card runs nothing at all. `HEADROOM` is the share of a card a
model may take, and it is settled as an exact integer inequality — `memory_mb * 100
<= gpu_memory_mb * HEADROOM` — because a ratio carrying a decimal point is one
rounding away from admitting a model the card cannot hold. Every one of those is a
*reason* rather than an exception: deciding what to run is the job this stage
describes, so the answer is data.

Then the queue. Once a variant is on a card, what is left is throughput: the model
serves a fixed number of tokens per tick, callers submit work with a tick of their
own, and the deployment has a small queue and a caller's patience (`BUDGET_TICKS`).
A submission that would wait longer than that is refused — returned, per
submission, naming why — and the refused submission never occupies a slot a
servable one needed, which is why the checks run in the order they do. A zone whose
egress policy reaches `"public"` may not serve at all: nothing is dequeued.

    QUEUE_MAX                  the submissions the queue holds at once (4)
    BUDGET_TICKS               the ticks a submission may wait for, inclusive (3)
    SUBMISSION_KEYS            the five fields of a submission, in order
    SERVE_REASONS              the four reasons a scheduler refuses a submission
    EdgeError                  the edge's refusal: a shape it cannot accept

    place(models, nodes, zone) -> (model, node, None) | (None, None, reason)
    Scheduler(model, node, network, zone)      one variant on one machine, in one zone
    Scheduler.submit(name, tokens, tick)       -> SUBMISSION_KEYS, queued or refused
    Scheduler.drain(tick)                      -> the SUBMISSION_KEYS one tick served
    Scheduler.queue()                          -> the queued submissions, in order
    Scheduler.served()                         -> the names served, in service order
    Scheduler.refused()                        -> (name, reason) pairs, in refusal order

DESIGN DECISION — why is the headroom rule an integer inequality with the boundary
inclusive?
Because "90% of the card" has to mean one thing for every card. `7200` megabytes on
an `8000` megabyte card is exactly 90% and must fit; `7201` must not, and no
floating-point division may decide that. Multiplying both sides by a hundred keeps
the comparison exact while the numbers stay whole, and it is the *card's* memory
that is compared, never the machine's RAM — a node with 128 GB of RAM and an 8 GB
card can still only hold an 8 GB model, and the mistake of reaching for
`memory_mb` (the node's) instead of `gpu_memory_mb` is precisely the mistake that
makes a deployment that runs beautifully on the FDE's laptop fail on the customer's.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `fits` answer `unknown-model` for a name instead of
looking one up?
Because `fits` holds no catalogue, and a function that invented one would be
inventing a customer. `fits(model, node)` is answered from two records and nothing
else: hand it a record and it judges the record, hand it a *name* and the honest
answer is that this function cannot see any model by that name — the caller has
handed it a label where the thing itself belongs. The `Scheduler` is where a name
meets the catalogue, because the `Scheduler` is the one thing holding the network;
the split is what keeps "does this fit" answerable on the back of an envelope while
"may this serve" stays a question about the customer's basement.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the zone decided by `place` and the `Scheduler` rather
than inside `fits`?
Because a zone is only wrong *relative to a request*. A node knows its own zone and
nothing about which zone was asked for, so a two-argument `fits` that answered
`zone` would be pretending to a fact it does not have. `place(models, nodes, zone)`
has the request, so the zone filter and the `zone` reason live there: a node in
another zone is not a candidate at all, and when no node in the requested zone
exists at all, that is the reason the answer carries.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a submission checked against the queue's capacity before
its own wait, and both before it is counted into the queue?
Because a full queue cannot accept the submission at all — that is a fact about the
queue — while the wait is a fact about this submission, and a refusal that had
already taken a slot would be a submission nobody ever serves, blocking a servable
one behind it. So the ladder is ordered (egress, then an unknown model, then
capacity, then budget), the budget is judged from the work already ahead of the
submission plus its own tokens, and the refusal is returned as data: `state`
`"refused"`, no queue entry, and a line in `refused()`.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `drain` spend exactly one tick of the model's throughput?
Because `tokens_per_tick` is what the model does in a tick, and a tick is the only
time there is. A `drain` that emptied the queue would make the reported `waiting`
meaningless and the budget unreachable: every submission would be served the moment
it arrived and a wait could never exceed a tick. Serving up to `tokens_per_tick`
tokens per call, in submission order, with a submission completed only when its own
last token is spent, is what makes "the ticks it has waited" a measurement rather
than a decoration — and it is why a submission larger than one tick's worth is
servable at all.

integer headroom ladder, the placement ordered by quality and its name tie-break,
and the scheduler with its submit, its one-tick drain, its queue, its served names
and its refusals.

import network

FIT_REASONS = ("unknown-model", "unknown-node", "no-gpu", "gpu-memory",
               "unknown-quant", "zone")
HEADROOM = 90
QUEUE_MAX = 4
BUDGET_TICKS = 3
SUBMISSION_KEYS = ("name", "tokens", "tick", "state", "waiting")
SERVE_REASONS = ("no-capacity", "budget", "egress", "unknown-model")


class EdgeError(estate.EstateError):
    """The edge's refusal: a shape it cannot accept, and nothing about the weather."""


def fits(model, node):
    """Whether a model variant fits a machine, as `(True, None)` or `(False, reason)`.

    `model` and `node` are `MODEL_KEYS` and `NODE_KEYS` records; a name handed where
    a record belongs is `unknown-model` or `unknown-node`, because this function
    holds no catalogue to look one up in. The ladder is the node's card, the
    quantisation, then the integer headroom rule, and the reason names the rung that
    said no.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement fits()")


def place(models, nodes, zone):
    """The best model a zone can run: `(model, node, None)` or `(None, None, reason)`.

    The model is the highest `quality`, ties broken by the higher `tokens_per_tick`
    and then by name, and its node is the first machine in `zone` it fits; when
    nothing fits, the reason is the one that kept the best model off the zone.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement place()")


class Scheduler:

    `model` and `node` are records or names the customer's own network holds, and
    `zone` is the zone this deployment serves. Construction is the wiring — a model
    that does not fit its node, a node of another zone or a zone that is not a zone
    are refused here, naming the offender, because no submission could make them
    right — while a *model* the network's catalogue does not hold is remembered and
    returned as the `unknown-model` serve reason on every submission.
    """

        `network` is the customer's own `network.Network`. A submission asks about
        this deployment, so everything that cannot be a deployment — the network,
        the zone, the node, the fit — is refused here, by name; only a model the
        catalogue does not hold is deferred, because it has a serve reason of its own.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement Scheduler.__init__()")

    def submit(self, name, tokens, tick):

        Accepted work is `"queued"`; a submission that would wait more than
        `BUDGET_TICKS`, a full queue, a zone that reaches `"public"` and a model the
        catalogue does not hold are answered `"refused"` with the reason, and none of
        them takes a queue slot.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement Scheduler.submit()")

    def drain(self, tick):

    def queue(self):

        raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement Scheduler.queue()")

    def served(self):
        """The names served so far, in service order."""
        raise NotImplementedError("stage 8: implement Scheduler.served()")

    def refused(self):

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 9: What the AI did for this team, in hours and cents.

Eight stages built the thing; this one has to say what it was worth. A renewal
conversation is not held about prompts and tokens, it is held about hours saved and
cents spent on *their* tickets, per team and per day, and every number in it has to
be recomputable by the person asking. So this stage holds no state of its own: it is
a set of functions over `Meter.spans()`, the customer's own record, and every answer
is recounted from those spans at the moment it is asked for. `Meter.stats()` exists,
is tempting, and is not the input: a dashboard that reads a counter agrees with that
counter's bug forever, which is the argument stage 2's verification and stage 3's
reconciliation are both built on.

The unit of an ROI conversation is a resolution. One span is one request; a ticket
that appears twice in a day — two models answering for it, a retry — is one ticket
for that day, and a span whose ticket is empty is not a ticket at all, it is a
request nobody can bill to anything. Minutes are saved only by resolutions
(`MINUTES_SAVED` is the customer's own estimate of a human's time, per team), so a
meter full of unresolved tickets saves nobody's minutes however many cents it burned.
Cost per resolution is the day's cents over the day's tickets, and it is zero, not an
error, when nothing resolved: a day that spent money and resolved nothing is a
finding, and a report that raises instead of printing it has thrown the finding away.

The return on that spend is a whole percentage, and it is `None` when the spend was
zero. "Infinite ROI" is not a number this stage may print, and neither is a division
by zero: a day whose cost is zero has no ratio, and saying so is the honest answer.
The same instinct governs `anomalies` — a cost compared against a team's own mean
needs more than one day of history to have a mean at all — and the comparison is at
least the threshold, *inclusively*, because the boundary is the number the customer
will argue about, and a boundary nobody pinned is a boundary that moves.

`unattributed` is the last question and the uncomfortable one. A span belongs to a
team; a span whose team is not one the caller owns is a token that was spent for
nobody, and the answer names it in the meter's own order — tick, team, ticket — so
the customer can go and find out who spent it.

    ROLLUP_KEYS                           the six fields of a (team, model) row, in order
    DASHBOARD_KEYS                        the seven fields of one day's dashboard, in order
    RATE_CENTS_PER_MINUTE                 what one saved minute of the customer's time is worth
    ROI_BASIS                             the denominator of a percentage: this many is 100%
    ANOMALY_KEYS                          the five fields of one anomaly, in order
    MetricError(estate.EstateError)       the stage's refusal: a shape it cannot recount
    rollup(meter)                         -> one ROLLUP_KEYS row per (team, model), sorted
    team_day(meter, day)                  -> that day's rows, same shape, same sort
    dashboard(meter, day)                 -> DASHBOARD_KEYS, the day recounted from its spans
    anomalies(meter, day, ratio_percent)  -> ANOMALY_KEYS, one per team at or over the threshold
    unattributed(meter, teams)            -> (tick, team, ticket) for every span of a stranger team

DESIGN DECISION — why is every answer recounted from `spans()` rather than read out
of `stats()`?
Because the meter's counters and the spans they were counted from are one bug apart,
and the counter is the side that cannot be questioned. `stats()` is the meter's belief
about itself: it is recomputed from the same log, by the same hand, and a dashboard
that copies it inherits every mistake in it without ever disagreeing. Reading the
spans makes the dashboard a *measurement* of the record rather than a restatement of
it, and it lets the check hold the two side by side — the spans, summed by the course,
against the stats, summed by the world. Where they differ, the customer's own log is
the tie-breaker, which is exactly the position a dashboard should be in.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a ticket counted once per day, and not once per model, and
not once for all time?
Because the question being answered is "how much did this team get done today, and
what did it cost", and a model is how an answer was produced, not what was resolved.
Two models answering the same ticket in one day, or a retry of the same ticket,
resolved that ticket once; a ticket carried over into tomorrow is a different day's
resolution, and the day is the window the customer reviews — a month-long dedupe would
report fewer resolutions the longer the meter ran. So a resolution is a (day, ticket)
pair, and everything that counts resolutions or minutes counts pairs, never spans.

DESIGN DECISION — why is `roi_percent` `None` when the day cost nothing, and not a
very large number?
Because "infinite" is not a number a report may print. A percentage of an investment is
`return * ROI_BASIS // investment`, and at a zero investment the expression has no
answer that survives being put in a slide: a sentinel like a huge integer is a number
the VP will quote, and quoting it once ends the credibility of every other number on
the page. `None` is not a missing measurement here, it is a verdict — there was no
investment to have a return on — and the shape the contract asks for is a field that
can say so.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a team with one day of history never an anomaly?
Because the baseline would be the day itself, and nothing is ever an anomaly compared
with itself. A team first seen today can only be at 100% of its own mean; calling that
out trains the reader to ignore the report, and the reader who ignores the report is
the one who misses the real anomaly next week. The same reasoning covers a team whose
mean is zero: a baseline of nothing flags nothing, so a team that has spent no cents
over any of its days is passed over instead of divided by.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the anomaly rule compare with `>=` and report the observed
ratio rather than the threshold?
Because the threshold is the caller's and the ratio is the finding. A team at exactly
the threshold is at the number the caller said to look at, so it is in the report;
excluding it is a boundary the check would have to pin on one side only, and a
one-sided boundary is where a defect hides. And a row that echoes the caller's own
constant back tells the reader nothing he did not type — the number worth carrying is
how far past the mean the day actually went, so `ratio_percent` is that observed
percentage, computed the same way the comparison is, in whole numbers.

TODO: implement `MetricError`, `rollup`, `team_day`, `dashboard`, `anomalies` and
`unattributed` in this file: the refusal, the per-(team, model) rollup, the same rows
for one day, the day's dashboard with its two divisions, the anomaly rule with its
baseline, and the spans whose team nobody claimed.
"""

import estate
import meter

ROLLUP_KEYS = ("team", "model", "spans", "cost_cents", "minutes_saved", "resolved")

DASHBOARD_KEYS = ("day", "teams", "cost_cents", "minutes_saved", "resolved",
                  "cost_per_resolution_cents", "roi_percent")

ANOMALY_KEYS = ("team", "day", "cost_cents", "baseline_cents", "ratio_percent")

RATE_CENTS_PER_MINUTE = 45

ROI_BASIS = 100


class MetricError(estate.EstateError):
    """The metric's refusal: something that cannot be counted at all.

    A shape mismatch — a meter that cannot answer `spans()`, a day that is not a
    whole number, a threshold that is not a percentage, teams that are not a tuple
    of team names — raises this, naming the offender, and never returns.
    """


def rollup(meter):
    """One `ROLLUP_KEYS` row per (team, model) pair the meter's spans mention.

    Sorted by (team, model): `spans` is how many spans the pair has, `cost_cents`
    what they cost, and `resolved` the tickets the pair resolved — a (day, ticket)
    pair the meter recorded as resolved, counted once however many spans carry it,
    with the empty ticket not a ticket at all. `minutes_saved` is those resolutions
    times the customer's own `MINUTES_SAVED` for the team.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement rollup()")


def team_day(meter, day):
    """The `ROLLUP_KEYS` rows for one day: the rollup of that day's spans only.

    A day is `tick // estate.TICKS_PER_DAY`, the same arithmetic the customer's
    own record uses; a day no span reached is an empty tuple, not a zero row.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement team_day()")


def dashboard(meter, day):
    """One day, recounted from its spans, as `DASHBOARD_KEYS`.

    `teams` is sorted; `cost_cents`, `minutes_saved` and `resolved` are the day's
    own totals, with a resolution the same (team, ticket) once; `resolved` is the
    number of tickets resolved that day; `cost_per_resolution_cents` is the day's
    cents over them and `0` when nothing resolved; `roi_percent` is
    `minutes_saved * RATE_CENTS_PER_MINUTE * ROI_BASIS // cost_cents`, and `None`
    when the day cost nothing, because a zero investment has no return to report.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement dashboard()")


def anomalies(meter, day, ratio_percent):
    """The teams whose cost on `day` is at least `ratio_percent` of their own mean.

    Sorted by team. A team's mean is over the days it has spans in — the days
    present in the meter for *that team* — and a team with fewer than two such
    days, or a mean of zero, is never an anomaly: there is no baseline to stand
    out from. The comparison is inclusive; `ratio_percent` in each row is the
    ratio observed, in whole percent.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement anomalies()")


def unattributed(meter, teams):
    """The spans whose team is not in `teams`, as `(tick, team, ticket)`.

    In the meter's own span order; `teams` is a tuple of team names, and anything
    that is not one raises rather than being iterated as if it were.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement unattributed()")
