"""FDE From Scratch — stage 10: Shadow traffic and a verdict.

A generic benchmark convinces nobody: it was not their tickets, not their
invoices and not their customers. So the candidate model is put on the
customer's own cases — and while it is there it must be *invisible*. Shadow
traffic is the discipline of measuring a model without letting it answer
anybody: every case goes to the incumbent and to the candidate, the user keeps
seeing what the user always saw, and the candidate's answer is filed beside the
incumbent's instead of being served. The first thing this stage can prove is
the one thing that must never happen: nothing the candidate answered reached
the user.

The second half is the part an eval project usually skips. A score is a
measurement, and a measurement is only as good as its instrument and its
sample: `grade` counts a model's accuracy over the cases that model *answered*
(a model that skipped the hard cases does not get to call them correct, and it
does not get them in its denominator either), `calibrate` measures the judge
itself against a sample a human labelled, and `verdict` refuses to decide until
the judge is trustworthy and the sample is large enough — before it looks at
the number everybody wanted to ship on.

    CASE_KEYS                          a customer case: its id, team, text, expected answer, class
    SHADOW_KEYS                        a shadow row: the case, both models' answers, what the user saw, whether they agreed
    GRADE_KEYS                         one model's marks: correct, total answered, accuracy in basis points
    AGREEMENT_KEYS                     the judge's calibration: agree, disagree, agreement in basis points
    VERDICTS                           the three words a verdict can be: "ship", "hold", "reject"
    VERDICT_REASONS                    why it is that word: "below-target", "judge-unreliable", "sample-too-small", "candidate-worse"
    MIN_SAMPLE                         the smallest sample a verdict may be based on
    MIN_AGREEMENT_BP                   the agreement a judge must reach before its verdicts count
    EvalError                          the shape refusal of this stage, a kind of estate.EstateError
    shadow(cases, incumbent, candidate, replay) -> tuple of SHADOW_KEYS, in case order
    grade(rows, cases) -> tuple of GRADE_KEYS, sorted by model
    calibrate(judge, labelled) -> AGREEMENT_KEYS
    verdict(grades, agreement, sample, target_bp) -> (verdict, reason or None)
    user_visible(rows) -> (case id, answer) per case, in case order

`shadow` calls `incumbent`, `candidate` and `replay` once per case, with the
case's own `text`, and each answers a string or `None` for a case it did not
answer. `grade` marks the two models against the labelled sample it is handed;
`calibrate` marks the judge against the labels a human wrote; `verdict` turns
both marks and a sample size into one of `VERDICTS` and, when the answer is not
a clean ship, into one reason from `VERDICT_REASONS`.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `user_sees` record the replay's answer and not the
candidate's?
Because a shadow run that leaks is worse than no eval at all: the candidate is
unproven, and the customer's users would be the ones finding out. So the row
does not merely *claim* the user was served by the incumbent — it carries the
answer the replay actually produced, which is the third callable's own answer
and never a copy of whatever the candidate said. A run whose `user_sees` equals
the candidate's answer is a run that served the candidate, and no amount of
accuracy makes that acceptable.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the accuracy denominator the cases a model answered,
and not the labelled sample?
Because the two are different questions, and only one of them is honest. Over
the labelled sample, a model that answered the four easy cases and skipped the
two hard ones is scored on six and punished for work it never did; over the
cases it answered, it is scored on four and the skipped cases are visible in
`total`, where a reader can see that the denominator moved. A model that
answered nothing is `total` 0 and `accuracy_bp` 0: the sample it was measured
on is empty, and an empty sample has no accuracy to report.

DESIGN DECISION — why are the judge's reliability and the sample size decided
before the target is consulted?
Because a decision has to be able to say "not yet" before it says "no". If the
target were consulted first, a candidate that missed it would come back
`reject` on a judge nobody calibrated and twenty cases nobody can generalize
from — a confident wrong answer, which is the expensive kind. Judge first (the
instrument), sample second (the measurement), target last (the comparison): a
verdict is only as trustworthy as the weakest thing it rests on.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a judge that gave no verdict count as a
disagreement rather than being skipped?
Because a judge that abstains on the cases it is unsure about would otherwise
look better the more it abstains: skip the misses and the agreement rises
toward certainty. The labelled sample is the denominator, the judge was asked
about every case in it, and "I have no verdict" is not an agreement with the
human's label — it is a failure to reach one, and it is counted as one.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `verdict` return a reason rather than a bare word?
Because "hold" means nothing on its own. The person who has to decide whether
to spend another two weeks needs to know which of the four things is the
blocker: the candidate is worse than an incumbent that was already good enough,
the whole project is below what the customer asked for, the judge cannot be
trusted, or there is simply not enough evidence yet — and the last two are the
reasons that send you back to collect more rather than back to the drawing
board.

this file: the shadow run that serves the replay's answer and files both
models', the marks over the cases a model answered, the calibration of the
judge against a human's labels, the verdict with its precedence, and the list
of what the user actually saw.
"""

CASE_KEYS = ("id", "team", "text", "expected", "class")

SHADOW_KEYS = ("id", "incumbent", "candidate", "user_sees", "same")

GRADE_KEYS = ("model", "correct", "total", "accuracy_bp")

AGREEMENT_KEYS = ("agree", "disagree", "agreement_bp")

VERDICTS = ("ship", "hold", "reject")

VERDICT_REASONS = ("below-target", "judge-unreliable", "sample-too-small",

MIN_SAMPLE = 30

MIN_AGREEMENT_BP = 8000

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement shadow()")

    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement grade()")

    """How far the judge can be trusted, against a sample a human labelled."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement calibrate()")


def verdict(grades, agreement, sample, target_bp):
    """The one-word answer, with the reason it is that word."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement verdict()")


def user_visible(rows):
    """`(case id, answer)` per case, in the cases' own order: what the user saw."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 10: implement user_visible()")

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 11: From a vague ask to a scoped four weeks.

Everything up to here has been a machine doing what a document said. This stage
is the document. A room full of people says things — an ask, a constraint, a
metric somebody already tracks, an objection, something deliberately ruled out —
and the FDE's job is the translation between what was said and what four weeks
of engineering can honestly promise. That translation is a data structure, and
this stage builds it: a transcript of statements in, a plan out, and every gap
between the two named rather than smoothed over.

The whole stage turns on one habit. A plan that quietly drops the ask nobody
owns, or the metric nobody ever measured, is smaller than the ask and looks
complete; a plan that keeps the requirement and says `no-owner` is the document
the customer can argue with. So a problem is never a deletion, the owner is the
speaker or nothing at all, and the priority is the word the customer chose.

    STATEMENT_KEYS    the six fields of one statement, in the order it is read
    KINDS             what a statement may be: ask, constraint, metric, objection, scope-out
    REQUIREMENT_KEYS  the six fields of a requirement, in order
    PRIORITIES        must, should, could — strongest first
    UNITS             the units a baseline may be measured in
    METRIC_KEYS       the four fields of a metric, in order
    PLAN_KEYS         the eight fields of the plan, in order
    WEEK_CAPACITY     how many requirements one week of the four holds
    MIN_WORDS         the fewest words an ask can be made of and still be one
    SCOPE_PROBLEMS    every gap a plan reports, in the order it reports them
    ScopeError        a transcript or a plan this course cannot read
    requirements      (transcript) -> the requirements, req-01, req-02… in order
    workstreams       (requirements) -> (owner, (ids)) sorted by owner
    schedule          (workstreams, weeks) -> weeks of owners in fill order
    metrics           (transcript) -> the metrics the customer already tracks
    scope             (transcript, customer, weeks) -> the plan
    sow               (plan) -> the text the customer is asked to sign

A statement is a mapping in `STATEMENT_KEYS` order. Its `kind` decides what it
is: an `ask`, a `constraint` and a `metric` are requirements, an `objection` is
context, and a `scope-out` is exile — a requirement whose text is exactly a
scope-out statement's text is the customer saying this was already ruled out. A
`metric` statement's `metric` field is a `METRIC_KEYS` mapping, while an ask's or
a constraint's is the metric's *name* or `None`. A requirement that has no owner,
no metric, or fewer than `MIN_WORDS` words is still a requirement, and its gap is
reported in `PLAN_KEYS["problems"]` as a `(problem, requirement id)` pair.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a requirement with a gap stay in the plan?
Because the plan is the thing the customer reads back. Dropping the ask with no
owner makes the document look finished and the scoping look smaller than it is,
and the gap — the thing somebody has to go and fix — disappears at exactly the
moment it becomes the FDE's job. Keeping it costs one line and turns a silent
omission into the first agenda item.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the priority read from the customer's own words rather
than from the seat the speaker sits in?
Because a title is not evidence about the work; it is evidence about the org
chart. An executive who says "maybe we should look at this" and an intern who
says "we must fix this" have told the FDE two different things, and an FDE who
reads the org chart instead of the sentence builds the wrong four weeks. The
sentence is what was said; the seat is what an outsider assumes.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a requirement's owner `None` rather than the FDE?
Because the FDE is the one owner that means nothing: nobody at the customer has
agreed to anything, and the work has no one to be handed to. Writing this
stage's own author into the field would fill the column and hide the gap that
`no-owner` exists to raise, and the whole handoff story of this course is about
the customer owning their own work.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `schedule` answer exactly `weeks` tuples even when the
work does not fit?
Because a schedule is a statement about capacity, not a wish. The weeks the
caller asked for are the weeks the customer has, so the answer has that length
and the overflow is not squeezed in — a week that holds four requirements is a

"""FDE From Scratch — stage 12: A runbook that is tested, and an admin who is not you.

Eleven stages have built things the FDE can demonstrate to a customer. This one
builds the two artifacts that decide whether the customer still needs the FDE
next quarter: a runbook somebody else can follow, and an administrative path
somebody else can drive.

The runbook is data first and a test second. A procedure is a name, the condition
it is for, the actor it is written for — `"customer"` or `"fde"` — an ordered
list of steps and a rollback list. `run` executes each step against the system it
is handed, checks that step's `expect` *after* the step, and, when the
expectation fails, runs the rollback and answers `rolled-back`. A run that failed
with an empty rollback answers `failed`, because "we undid it" and "there was
nothing to undo it with" are different claims and only one of them is true. A
step whose `expect` is empty is applied and then cannot be verified at all: the
run does not get to call that a pass, and the runbook reports it as a problem.

The test is the drill, and a drill injects a *fault*: a procedure, the index of a
step of that procedure, and the answer the system will be made to give at that
step. The system is still called — the fault does not reach into it, it replaces
what came back — which is what makes a drill a rehearsal of the runbook rather
than a rehearsal of the customer's luck. `drill` answers one row per `(procedure,
fault)`: that procedure run with that fault armed, the row's `fault` being the
fault's step. Every procedure no fault names gets one row with `fault` `None` and
the outcome `uncovered`, because the good news is not the product of a drill —
`uncovered` is. A procedure that no fault exercises has never been run for real,
and the only thing worse than a runbook nobody tested is a runbook everybody
believes was tested.

`gaps` turns that report, plus the runbook's own actors, into the leverage list:
the procedures no fault exercised, and the procedures still written for the FDE.
Leverage is measured by how little the customer needs you, so a procedure written
for the FDE is a gap even when it passes its drill, and a procedure both
untested and FDE-only is reported as untested first.

The admin is the second half of the same idea: the customer's operators need a
path that is theirs, and that path has to be auditable. `Admin.change` answers
`applied` only for an actor whose rights carry the action's own right, and writes
one `ADMIN_KEYS` line for every attempt, allowed or refused — the refused ones are
the ones an auditor asks about. `Admin.dry_run` answers the string the system
*would* give without touching the system at all: the rehearsal runs against a copy,
so an operator can see what would happen before anything happens.

    PROCEDURE_KEYS                     the five fields of a procedure, in order
    STEP_KEYS                          the three fields of a step, in order
    ACTORS                             the two actors a procedure can be written for
    OUTCOMES                           what a procedure can be, once it is exercised
    DRILL_KEYS                         the three fields of a drill row, in order
    FAULT_KEYS                         the three fields of a fault, in order
    ADMIN_KEYS                         the six fields of an admin line, in order
    RUN_KEYS                           the four fields of a run, in order
    RUNBOOK_PROBLEMS                   what a runbook cannot vouch for, in precedence order
    GAP_REASONS                        why a procedure is on the leverage list
    RunbookError                       every refusal this stage raises
    Runbook()                          an empty runbook: no procedures, no problems
    Runbook.add(procedure)             -> PROCEDURE_KEYS, the record the runbook holds
    Runbook.procedures()               -> the names it holds, sorted
    Runbook.problems()                 -> (name, problem) pairs, in RUNBOOK_PROBLEMS order
    Runbook.run(name, system, tick)    -> RUN_KEYS, one procedure against one system
    Runbook.drill(faults, system, tick)-> DRILL_KEYS rows, sorted by (procedure, fault)
    Runbook.self_serve()               -> the procedures written for the customer, sorted
    Admin(system, rights)              one system, and who may apply what to it
    Admin.change(action, target, value, actor, tick) -> ADMIN_KEYS, and one log line
    Admin.dry_run(action, target, value)             -> what the system would answer
    Admin.log()                        -> every attempt this admin made, in order
    gaps(drill_report, runbook)        -> (procedure, reason) pairs, sorted

A system is any object with `apply(action, target, value) -> str` and
`state() -> dict`: the stage calls it and never reaches into it. A step hands its
own `expect` to `apply` as the value — a step says what the target should answer —
and a rollback step is applied the same way and is not verified, because a
recovery that answers something other than what it hoped for is still the recovery
that ran.

DESIGN DECISION — why are `rolled-back` and `failed` different answers, when both
say the run did not work?
Because they are the two different things an operator has to do next. `rolled-back`
means the system was put back and the incident stands as it was; `failed` means the
procedure stopped half-applied with nothing to put anything back with, and that is
the answer that has to wake somebody up. Collapsing them into one outcome would hide
the only distinction the runbook exists to make — the runbook that cannot undo itself
is the runbook you must not hand over.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a fault replace the answer instead of breaking the
system?
Because a drill has to be reproducible, and breaking a real system is not. A fault
names one step of one procedure and the answer that step will be made to receive;
the system is still called, so the drill exercises the same code path as a real run
and the runbook sees exactly what a real fault would hand it, while the injected
answer is data the caller chose and can therefore be asserted. A drill that reached
into the system to make it fail would depend on the system's own internals, would
leave the system changed for every procedure after it, and could not be run twice
for the same result.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a step with an empty `expect` a failure rather than a
skip?
Because a skip is a pass with a footnote. If an unverified step let the run continue
and report `recovered`, the runbook would be claiming a recovery it never confirmed,
and the claim would be indistinguishable from one it did confirm — the exact
substitution this course exists to refuse. So the step is applied, the absence of an
expectation is recorded as a problem of the procedure, and the run takes the failure
path: a procedure that cannot be verified is not a procedure that passed.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `dry_run` rehearse against a copy rather than apply and
undo?
Because there is no undo. The protocol gives this stage `apply` and `state` and
nothing else: an action that has run cannot be un-run by anything the stage knows,
and reverse-engineering one from `state()` would be guessing at a system this stage
does not own. A copy can be asked exactly what the system would answer — same code,
same question — while the system itself is never touched, which is what makes the
answer a *rehearsal* rather than a change somebody has to remember to reverse.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a procedure that is both untested and FDE-only report
`uncovered`?
Because the untested fact is the one that changes the handoff. Both are gaps and
neither is good news, but `fde-only` says "the customer has not taken this over
yet", while `uncovered` says "nobody knows whether this works at all" — and handing
over a procedure nobody has ever exercised is how a customer inherits a runbook that
fails on its first real incident. The report names the worse gap, so the work list
starts where the risk is.

reports what nobody exercised, the admin with its rights and its log, and the
dry run that leaves the system exactly as it found it.
"""

import estate

PROCEDURE_KEYS = ("name", "when", "actor", "steps", "rollback")

STEP_KEYS = ("action", "target", "expect")

ACTORS = ("customer", "fde")

OUTCOMES = ("recovered", "rolled-back", "uncovered", "failed")

DRILL_KEYS = ("procedure", "fault", "outcome")

FAULT_KEYS = ("procedure", "step", "answer")

ADMIN_KEYS = ("actor", "action", "target", "value", "tick", "verdict")

RUN_KEYS = ("procedure", "outcome", "steps_done", "rollback_done")

"""The tiny API an authored course uses to describe its stages.

A course is a directory containing `course.py`:

    from codecraft.api import stage

    TITLE = "Build a Bloom Filter"
    DESCRIPTION = "A probabilistic set, from hashing to false-positive math."

    def check_1():
        from bloom import BloomFilter
        bf = BloomFilter(bits=64, hashes=2)
        bf.add("x")
        assert "x" in bf
        assert "y" not in bf, "a fresh filter must not report false members"

    STAGES = [
        stage(
            1,
            file="bloom.py",
            title="add and contains",
            tags=["hashing", "data-structure"],
            action="Implement add() to set the k bit positions.",
            predict="can contains() ever be certain an item is absent?",
            hints=["bits = bits[:] to avoid shared state",
                   "use one hash salt per position"],
            check=check_1,
        ),
        ...
    ]

`codecraft run <course>` imports this file, runs each `check`, records the
attempt, and hands the result to the adaptive engine. `hints` are optional —
when omitted, the engine generates them from `action`/`predict`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional


@dataclass
class Stage:
    id: int
    file: str
    title: str
    check: Callable[[], None]
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action: str = ""
    predict: str = ""
    hints: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    solution: Optional[str] = None   # e.g. "solutions/bloom.py: BloomFilter.add"

    def meta(self) -> Dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "file": self.file,
            "title": self.title,
            "tags": list(self.tags),
            "action": self.action,
            "predict": self.predict,
            "hints": list(self.hints),
            "solution": self.solution,
        }


def stage(id: int, file: str, title: str, check: Callable[[], None],
          tags: Optional[List[str]] = None, action: str = "", predict: str = "",
          hints: Optional[List[str]] = None,
          solution: Optional[str] = None) -> Stage:
    """Convenience constructor so course.py stays readable."""
    return Stage(
        id=id, file=file, title=title, check=check, tags=list(tags or []),
        action=action, predict=predict, hints=list(hints or []),
        solution=solution,
    )
